title: The Signal from the Target Travels Home

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: In young target-dependent neurons, the new gene transcription needed for death after NGF loss occurs in the {{c1::nucleus}}.
cards.back: A survival signal received at a distant axon terminal must therefore influence the cell body.
cards.quote: the death that follows loss of NGF needs new genes switched on in the nucleus

cards.front: Why is binding a survival factor at a distant axon terminal insufficient to establish that it can keep a target-dependent neuron alive?
cards.back: Its signal must reach the cell body and still be able to signal there; terminal binding alone establishes neither requirement.
cards.quote: A target keeps a neuron alive only if its signal makes the trip home and is able to signal when it gets there.

cards.front: A factor stimulates growth at a distant axon terminal but produces no signal at the cell body. Can terminal treatment alone support survival of a target-dependent neuron, and why?
cards.back: No. Local growth can occur where the factor acts, but survival supported from the terminal requires a signal that reaches and acts on the cell body.
cards.quote: Local effects, such as axon growth where the factor is, do not need the trip, and a factor given straight to the cell body bypasses it.

cards.front: For diffusion at a fixed diffusion coefficient, typical travel time grows with the {{c1::square}} of the distance.
cards.back: The approximation is time ≈ distance² / (2 × D).
cards.quote: The typical time to diffuse a distance grows with the square of that distance.

cards.front: Why does diffusion fail to deliver a useful protein phosphorylation signal along a centimetre-long sympathetic axon?
cards.back: Diffusion takes far too long, and phosphatases remove the signaling phosphates along the way. Protein arrival need not mean arrival of an active signal.
cards.quote: Protein molecules may still drift in, but inactive: the signal does not arrive late, it arrives switched off.

cards.front: Estimate a protein’s diffusion time over a 1 cm sympathetic axon using D ≈ 10 µm²/s and t ≈ L²/(2D). Give seconds and approximate days.
cards.back: L = 10,000 µm. t ≈ (10,000 µm)² / (2 × 10 µm²/s) = 5,000,000 s; dividing by 86,400 s/day gives about 58 days, roughly two months.
cards.quote: 10,000 squared is 10⁸, and 10⁸ / 20 is about 5 million seconds: roughly two months.

cards.front: Two axons have the same cytoplasmic diffusion coefficient, but one is three times as long. How does typical protein diffusion time compare, and why?
cards.back: It is nine times longer in the longer axon, because diffusion time scales with distance squared: 3² = 9.
cards.quote: The typical time to diffuse a distance grows with the square of that distance.

cards.front: Enzymes that remove the phosphates carried by many intracellular protein signals are called {{c1::phosphatases}}.
cards.back: Removing a signaling phosphate can switch the signal off.
cards.quote: Many signals inside a cell are proteins carrying an added phosphate, and enzymes called phosphatases keep removing those phosphates.

cards.front: In an illustrative diffusion model, the active signal’s fade distance is √(D × lifetime). With D = 10 µm²/s and phosphate lifetime = 10 s, what is that distance?
cards.back: √[(10 µm²/s) × (10 s)] = √(100 µm²) = 10 µm. These illustrative rates are not measured TrkA pathway values.
cards.quote: The active signal then fades over a distance of about √(D × lifetime) = √(10 × 10) = 10 micrometres:

cards.front: Beyond remaining able to signal on arrival, what message-preserving property should a long-distance axonal signal have?
cards.back: It should keep the target’s message separate from signals encountered along the axon. Keeping ligand bound to receptor is one possible way.
cards.quote: It should keep the target's message separate from signals the neuron picks up along the way.

cards.front: The NGF receptor TrkA belongs to the {{c1::receptor tyrosine kinase}} class.
cards.back: Its phosphorylated tails recruit signaling proteins.
cards.quote: TrkA is a receptor tyrosine kinase: an NGF dimer holds two TrkA molecules together, their kinases add phosphates to each other's tyrosines

cards.front: How does ligand-driven pairing activate a receptor tyrosine kinase, as illustrated by NGF binding TrkA?
cards.back: The ligand holds two receptors together. Their kinases phosphorylate each other’s tyrosines, creating phosphorylated tails that recruit signaling proteins.
cards.quote: their kinases add phosphates to each other's tyrosines, and the phosphorylated tails recruit signaling proteins.

cards.front: In the favored model of retrograde NGF signaling, what is a signaling endosome?
cards.back: A small membrane vesicle containing internalized NGF bound to active TrkA.
cards.quote: The ligand and the active receptor are pulled into the cell together in a small membrane vesicle, the signaling endosome.

cards.front: In the retrograde endosome model, {{c1::dynein}} carries vesicles along microtubules toward the neuronal cell body.
cards.back: This provides directed transport from the axon terminal.
cards.quote: The motor protein dynein drags it along microtubules toward the cell body.

cards.front: How can an internalized NGF-TrkA complex signal to cytoplasmic proteins while it is inside an endosome?
cards.back: NGF stays bound inside the vesicle, while TrkA’s kinase tails face the cytoplasm, where they can continue signaling.
cards.quote: NGF stays bound inside the vesicle, while TrkA's kinase tails face the cytoplasm outside it,

cards.front: An endosome travels 3 cm along a sympathetic axon at a constant 1 µm/s without pausing. Estimate its travel time in hours.
cards.quote: Dynein-driven endosomes move at roughly a micrometre per second, so a centimetre takes about three hours.

cards.front: In an illustrative transport model, a complex permanently loses signaling competence with a half-life of 1 hour and cannot reactivate. What fraction remains competent after a 3-hour trip?
cards.back: Fraction = (1/2)^(trip time/half-life) = (1/2)^(3 h/1 h) = 1/8 = 12.5%. Transport alone does not guarantee signaling competence on arrival.
cards.quote: If it halves every hour, a three-hour trip is three halvings: (1/2)³ = 1/8 arrive able to signal.

cards.front: In the chick leg experiment with radiolabeled NGF, what labeling pattern would support leakage into blood rather than the reported selective transport?
cards.back: Label reaching both sides would support blood-borne spread. The reported same-side sensory-ganglion labeling, with the motor column unlabeled, instead supports selective uptake and transport.
cards.quote: Label leaking into the blood would reach both sides; uptake by any nerve would label the motor column.

cards.front: Radioactive label from a protein applied to an axon terminal later appears in the cell body. Why does that alone fail to establish delivery of a functional survival signal?
cards.back: Radioactivity locates label; it does not establish that the protein arrived intact, remained active, or contributed to survival.
cards.quote: It cannot tell you whether NGF arrived intact, whether it was active, or whether its arrival had anything to do with survival.

cards.front: What feature of Campenot’s compartmented neuronal cultures lets investigators expose distal axons and cell bodies to different media?
cards.back: A sealed divider separates the chambers so their fluids do not mix, while axons grow under the seal.
cards.quote: a divider, sealed to the dish, separated a central chamber from side chambers.

cards.front: In compartmented rat sympathetic cultures, a treatment removes available NGF from one distal-axon chamber while cell-body NGF is maintained. What happens locally, and why?
cards.back: Axons in the treated chamber stop growing and later degenerate. Cell-body NGF does not replace the NGF those axons need in their own surroundings.
cards.quote: the axons there stopped growing and later degenerated, even though their cell bodies sat in NGF.

cards.front: What did survival of many sympathetic cell bodies supplied with NGF only through their distal-axon chamber establish?
cards.back: A signal originating in the distal axon can support cell-body survival. The experiment does not identify what carries that signal.
cards.quote: And when cell bodies had no NGF, many still survived, provided their axons reached a chamber that had it.

cards.front: Why does nuclear CREB phosphorylation after NGF treatment confined to distal sympathetic axons establish long-distance signaling without identifying its carrier?
cards.back: It shows that a distal signal reaches a nuclear transcription factor. Both a carried complex and a relay could produce that endpoint.
cards.quote: gave NGF only to the distal axons of cultured rat sympathetic neurons and found CREB phosphorylated in the nuclei.

cards.front: What distinguishes a courier model from a relay model of terminal-to-cell-body signaling?
cards.back: A courier carries the same signaling complex the whole way; a relay activates successive stretches without one molecule making the entire trip.
cards.quote: The NGF-TrkA complex itself is carried the whole way and signals when it arrives.

cards.front: Why can loss of neuronal survival after blocking a transport motor fail to distinguish a carried messenger from a relay?
cards.back: A relay may also require that motor at each local step. Blocking a component shared by both models cannot distinguish them.
cards.quote: A dynein block, by itself, cannot tell a courier from a relay.

cards.front: Design a compartmented sympathetic-neuron test that distinguishes a carried NGF-TrkA complex from a relay requiring TrkA kinase in every axonal stretch. State a crucial control and the interpretation.
cards.back: Inhibit TrkA kinase only in a middle axon segment, verifying inhibition without disrupting transport. Preserved cell-body signaling and survival favor the courier over that relay. Rule: a courier can reactivate after crossing; that relay requires kinase activity in every stretch. Other relays remain possible.
cards.quote: blocking TrkA kinase only in the middle stretch of the axon did not stop the signal reaching the cell bodies or the neurons' survival.

cards.front: A middle-axon TrkA inhibitor abolishes distal-NGF-supported survival, but imaging also shows that it stops endosome movement. Does this result favor a TrkA relay, and why?
cards.back: No clear distinction is possible. The treatment also disrupts the courier’s transport, so either model could explain the loss of survival.
cards.quote: That is evidence against a relay built from TrkA kinase, and for a courier, though not against every kind of relay.

cards.front: Live imaging shows labeled ligand-receptor complexes moving from an axon terminal to the cell body. Why is this insufficient to show that their movement causes neuronal survival?
cards.back: Imaging establishes carriage, but the moving complexes could be incidental to survival. Their causal role requires additional functional evidence.
cards.quote: Imaging shows that complexes are carried, not that they are what keeps the neuron alive.

cards.front: For developing mouse sympathetic axons, which factor comes from the blood vessels along the route, and which comes from the final targets?
cards.back: Intermediate blood vessels provide NT-3; final targets provide NGF.
cards.quote: The vessels, an intermediate target, make NT-3. The final targets make NGF.
cards.section: NGF versus NT-3: one signal makes the trip

cards.front: How can NGF and NT-3 both support local growth through TrkA, yet only distal NGF supports survival of cultured sympathetic cell bodies?
cards.back: Both activate TrkA locally, but only NGF-TrkA complexes are stably carried back. Local receptor activation does not establish delivery of a survival signal.
cards.quote: Both factors activate TrkA at the axon, so local signaling for growth works in both cases. The difference was in trafficking.
cards.section: NGF versus NT-3: one signal makes the trip

cards.front: In compartmented sympathetic cultures with no factor at the cell bodies, both NGF and NT-3 activate distal TrkA. If their different survival effects reflect trafficking, how should somatic phospho-TrkA and nuclear phospho-CREB compare?
cards.back: Both readouts should appear with distal NGF but neither with distal NT-3. Only the NGF-TrkA signal is stably carried to the cell body.
cards.quote: look for phosphorylated TrkA arriving in cell bodies, and for nuclear CREB phosphorylation, with each factor on the axons: both with NGF, neither with NT-3.
cards.section: NGF versus NT-3: one signal makes the trip

cards.front: How could the proposed NGF-driven increase in p75 help a developing sympathetic neuron switch from an intermediate target to its final target?
cards.back: Retrograde NGF signaling raises p75, and responsiveness to NT-3 falls as p75 rises. The neuron becomes less responsive to the intermediate target.
cards.quote: As p75 rises, the neuron's response to NT-3 falls, so the neuron becomes less responsive to the intermediate target once it reaches the final one.
cards.section: NGF versus NT-3: one signal makes the trip

cards.front: Suppose an intermediate-target factor now delivers a signaling-competent TrkA complex to a developing sympathetic cell body. What constraint on its ability to support survival has been removed, and what remains unproven?
cards.back: Failure to deliver a competent signal has been removed, so intermediate-target survival support becomes possible. Survival still needs testing: the rule requires arrival with signaling competence but does not guarantee that every arriving signal is sufficient.
cards.quote: A factor that acts only locally can steer an axon, and so decide which target it reaches, but it cannot by itself keep the neuron alive.
cards.section: NGF versus NT-3: one signal makes the trip

cards.front: Factor Y activates distal TrkA in sympathetic neurons but fails to support survival. How would you distinguish failure to carry the receptor from loss of its signaling competence during transport?
cards.back: Track distal-origin TrkA and its phosphorylation along the axon and in the cell body, using NGF as a comparison. No carried receptor points to uptake or sorting; carried receptor losing phosphorylation points to inactivation. Rule: ligand label alone does not establish delivery of a signaling-competent receptor.
cards.quote: No carried receptor points to uptake or sorting; carried receptor that fades points to switching off on the way.

cards.front: After distal factor Y treatment, active TrkA reaches sympathetic cell bodies, but nuclear CREB is not phosphorylated and neurons die. Where does this pattern place a failure?
cards.back: It points to a failure in the cell-body response after active receptor arrival, rather than failure to deliver active TrkA. CREB is one readout of that response.
cards.quote: Active TrkA in the cell bodies without phospho-CREB points here.

cards.front: A candidate survival factor fails when applied only to distal axons. Design a cell-body treatment control and explain what a positive result would and would not locate.
cards.back: Apply the factor directly to cell bodies at a matched dose. Survival shows that the neurons can use it and places the distal-treatment failure between terminal exposure and a sufficient cell-body response. Rule: direct cell-body delivery bypasses the trip; it does not identify which intervening step failed.
cards.quote: If the neurons then survive, they can use Y, so the failure lies somewhere between the axon tip and a sufficient response in the cell body.

cards.front: In young target-dependent neurons, is all death machinery confined to the cell body?
cards.back: No. Bcl-2 family proteins act at mitochondria, including those along axons; the nucleus needed for new death-program transcription is confined to the cell body.
cards.quote: The Bcl-2 family proteins act at mitochondria, and mitochondria run along the axon too;

cards.front: A neuronal response appears across a 1 mm axon within 1 minute. What minimum speed would a terminal-origin carrier need, and how does that compare with endosomes moving at roughly 1 µm/s?
cards.back: 1 mm = 1,000 µm; 1 min = 60 s. v ≥ 1,000/60 ≈ 16.7 µm/s, about 17 times 1 µm/s. Endosomes moving at roughly 1 µm/s cannot account for such rapid arrival.
cards.quote: Even across one millimetre, arriving within a minute would need about 17 micrometres per second, far above the roughly one micrometre per second measured for dynein transport.

cards.front: Bead-bound distal NGF supports rat sympathetic-neuron survival with little or no NGF transport, whereas another study requires internalization and transport for nuclear CREB phosphorylation. What conclusion respects both results?
cards.back: The bead result suggests survival may not require NGF itself to travel in those conditions. It does not resolve the CREB transport requirement or establish one universal mechanism. Rule: survival and nuclear CREB phosphorylation are different readouts, and an arriving signal alone does not guarantee a complete survival response.
cards.quote: The two studies measured different things, a nuclear transcription factor against survival, and how they fit together is part of the open question.

cards.front: In the reported study, Coronin-1 keeps NGF-TrkA endosomes from fusing with lysosomes. If this protection is lost, what change in signaling capacity would you predict, and what comparison would test that explanation?
cards.back: Reduced preservation of signaling-competent endosomes is expected. Compare endosome-lysosome fusion and cell-body signaling with and without Coronin-1 protection. Rules: Coronin-1 limits lysosomal fusion, and retrograde survival support requires a signal that reaches the cell body and can still signal there; carriage alone is insufficient.
cards.quote: an endosomal effector that keeps NGF-TrkA endosomes from fusing with lysosomes, and found that it is required for developmental competition for survival.
cards.section: Does a single flavor of endosome mediate all of these functions?
